clinicalPearls: A communication in the atrial septum permitting left-to-right shunting; the secundum type in the region of the fossa ovalis is the most common form.
Most children are asymptomatic and are detected through an incidental murmur or, later, right heart enlargement; heart failure in infancy is uncommon.

The characteristic auscultatory finding is a widely and fixedly split second heart sound, accompanied by a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from increased pulmonary flow.
A larger shunt may produce a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border from increased flow across the tricuspid valve.
The murmur reflects increased flow through the pulmonary valve rather than turbulent flow across the defect itself, which is low-velocity and inaudible.
Echocardiography defines the defect type and size, direction of shunt, and degree of right atrial and right ventricular volume overload.
Small secundum defects frequently close spontaneously in early childhood; a defect must be distinguished from a normal patent foramen ovale.
Significant defects are closed, often by transcatheter device for suitable secundum defects, to prevent later right heart enlargement, arrhythmias, and pulmonary vascular disease.
Untreated large defects may lead in adulthood to atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, and, rarely, paradoxical embolism.
reference.pathophysiology: An opening in the atrial septum allows blood to shunt from the higher-compliance left atrium toward the right atrium, the direction favoured because the right ventricle is more compliant than the left. This left-to-right shunt volume-loads the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary circulation while the left-sided output is maintained by the shunt returning through the lungs. Chronic volume overload dilates the right heart; over many years a minority develop elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension, and the resulting right atrial stretch predisposes to atrial arrhythmias.
additionalDifferentials: Patent foramen ovale (a normal variant, not a true defect)
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to define defect type, size, and right heart volume overload
Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in significant shunts
Electrocardiogram, often showing right axis deviation and right ventricular volume overload (rsR' pattern)
Transoesophageal echocardiography or advanced imaging when transthoracic views are inadequate
Cardiac catheterisation if pulmonary hypertension needs assessment
redFlags: Signs of significant right heart volume overload or pulmonary hypertension
Failure to thrive or heart failure in an infant, suggesting an additional or larger lesion
New cyanosis suggesting shunt reversal in longstanding, untreated disease
reference.prognosis: Isolated secundum defects, whether closed spontaneously, by device, or surgically, have an excellent outlook when addressed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Late, unrepaired large defects carry increasing risk of arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension in adulthood.
pitfalls: Mistaking a normal patent foramen ovale for a true atrial septal defect
Dismissing the subtle findings and missing a significant defect until right heart enlargement is advanced
Attributing fixed splitting of the second heart sound to a benign murmur
Assuming all defects require closure when many small secundum defects close spontaneously
Overlooking associated anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
management: Close a haemodynamically significant defect causing right heart volume overload, using transcatheter device occlusion for a suitable secundum defect and surgical repair for other morphologies
Observe small defects and those in infancy, allowing for possible spontaneous closure, and time intervention before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops
Relieve symptoms of heart failure with diuretics where present
Assess pulmonary vascular resistance when pulmonary hypertension is suspected and avoid closure once Eisenmenger physiology has developed
Monitor for atrial arrhythmias and progressive pulmonary hypertension over long-term follow-up
Provide ongoing paediatric and, later, adult congenital cardiology surveillance
